notes:
Now let me fetch the full Enduring Word and Pulpit pages.Below are verse-by-verse notes on Jeremiah 3. Every point has a citation and the page's web address.

**What I couldn't cover:** I ran out of searches and page reads before I reached any Catholic or Orthodox site (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), the NET Bible notes, or a Lutheran, Methodist-site or Pentecostal-site writer on this chapter. I also found no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. Those parts are left out. Precept Austin's page says everything after 3:10 is still unfinished.

**About the tradition labels:** StudyLight itself labels Ellicott "Arminian… Anglican." The other labels are the usual ones, not taken from the pages: Calvin (Reformed), Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist), Clarke (Methodist), Barnes (Presbyterian), Guzik (Calvary Chapel; enduringword.com is on your Pentecostal and charismatic list), Coffman (Churches of Christ).

---

**v. 1**
- **The background law.** The verse looks back to Deuteronomy 24:1–4, which says a divorced wife who has remarried may not go back to her first husband. Ellicott thinks the recent discovery of the Book of the Law had probably brought that law into prominence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
- **Why the law existed.** Guzik says it stopped people treating marriage and divorce lightly, as if one could divorce now and remarry later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
- **The main disagreement: invitation or rebuke?** Translators are split on the last line. Some take it as an invitation, others as an accusation that Israel wants to come back lightly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
  - *Read as an invitation:*
    - Guzik says God does keep inviting Israel back in the rest of the chapter, so it is best read as a plea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
    - Calvin reads it as pardon offered if the people repent. He argues from the lesser to the greater: God's kindness goes beyond anything people show each other. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
    - Ellicott also takes it as an invitation. He says it misreads Jeremiah to think he ever preached a condemnation that left no room for repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
    - Clarke says God, the first husband, is willing to take back the unfaithful wife if she gives up her idols. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
  - *Read as a rebuke:*
    - The Pulpit Commentary says most recent commentators translate it "And thinkest thou to return to me?" They see the very idea as unthinkable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
    - Barnes says the argument here is not about mercy. It proves that after so much adultery, Israel could not simply take her place as wife again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
    - Coffman agrees. He adds that the racial covenant with Israel ended for good, and that forgiveness now comes on New Covenant terms. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html

**v. 2**
- **"Barren heights."** These are the hilltop shrines of pagan gods. Guzik quotes Ryken: the word for "lain with" is a crude word for sexual violence, and false gods are always abusive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
- **A mirror, not a quick fix.** The Pulpit Commentary says no surface-level reform counts as returning to God. The prophet shows the sins that real repentance has to end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **"Like a nomad in the desert."** Coffman gives two readings: an Arab raider lying in wait for a caravan, or a prostitute sitting by the road (compare Tamar in Genesis 38). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html

**v. 3**
- **The drought.** Ellicott says disasters were seen as punishment for these sins, and there seems to have been a severe drought under Josiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-3.html
- **The irony.** Baal, the fertility god who was supposed to send rain, turned out to be powerless. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-3-commentary
- **"Brazen look."** Guzik says their conscience had stopped working. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/

**vv. 4–5**
- **Words without change.** The Pulpit Commentary says the prophet grants there was an apparent revival of faith during Josiah's forced reform, but denies it was more than apparent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **Fleming (Bridgeway Bible Commentary)** says Judah boldly asks God to act like an over-kind father, yet God will act justly against her sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html
- **Matthew Henry, quoted by Coffman,** takes "all the evil you can" to mean they would have done even worse if they had known how. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-1.html

**vv. 6–7**
- **Setting.** These words came under Josiah, a reforming king. Israel did not return and fell as a kingdom about 100 years before Jeremiah began to prophesy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-3.cfm

**v. 8**
- **What the divorce means.** GotQuestions says the "divorce" refers to the Assyrian invasion and Israel's removal from its land. It adds that God never cut Israel off for all time. https://www.gotquestions.org/did-God-divorce-Israel.html
- **Gill** says the Lord, married to this people, put them away into captivity (2 Kings 17:6), and that this captivity is the "bill of divorce." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/jeremiah/3-8.html
- **A wording problem in the Hebrew.** The Pulpit Commentary discusses whether to drop "and I saw" (as the Vulgate does) or to read "and she saw" (as Ewald does). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 9**
- **"Indifferent."** The Hebrew literally speaks of the "lightness" of her whoredom: she thought it of little importance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **"Stones and trees."** Utley at bible.org says this refers to Baal (male) and Asherah (female), the Canaanite gods. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-3

**v. 10**
- **"Only in pretense."** Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: Josiah's reforms were outward and did not touch the people deeply. He also warns that we should be generous when judging other people's repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
- **The Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes)** calls false repentance both inexcusable and useless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html

**v. 11**
- **Why Judah was worse.** The Pulpit Commentary says Judah had Israel's example as a warning and was guilty of hypocrisy, the most hateful of sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **Guzik's reasons:** Judah had Israel's example, was nearer the temple, and had better kings. Israel was more honest about its sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/

**v. 12**
- **"Toward the north."** The message goes to the northern exiles. The Pulpit Commentary notes how warmly Jeremiah still felt for them more than a hundred years after their kingdom fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **A wordplay.** Guzik quotes Thompson: the one who "turned away" is invited to "turn back." Guzik adds that the promise here is a restored relationship, not the return of the northern kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/

**v. 13**
- **The one condition.** The Pulpit Commentary says confessing is the condition, and it is enough: no sacrifice, penance or partial reform is required first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html
- **"Scattered your favors."** The Pulpit Commentary links this to Judah chasing foreign alliances (Jeremiah 2:36). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 14**
- **"I am your master."** Utley notes a play on the word Baal, which means "husband." https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-3
- **Still married.** Guzik notes the tension with verse 8: God says "I am married to you" and is willing to set the divorce aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
- **"One from a city, two from a family."** The Pulpit Commentary says God's promises are mainly to communities but he still cares specially for individuals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **The Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes)** draws a call for each person to return to God personally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html

**v. 15**
- **Shepherds after God's heart.** The Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes) says the real shepherd is whoever actually feeds the flock, whatever his official standing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html

**v. 16** (a verse where readings differ)
- **The ark will not be missed.** Ellicott calls this very bold and sees in it the seed of the New Covenant in Jeremiah 31:31. He contrasts it with the legend in 2 Maccabees 2:4–5 that Jeremiah hid the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/3-16.htm
- **Barnes** says the symbol passes away because God will live in his people by the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-16.html
- **Calvin** says almost all Christians have read it as the end of the law's "shadows" when Christ came. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-16.html
- **Where is this fulfilled?**
  - *In the Church:* Benson says Jerusalem here stands for the Christian Church, which becomes God's dwelling place instead of the ark. Gill applies the "multiplying" to believers in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/3-16.htm
  - *In a future kingdom:* Chuck Smith applies it to the "Kingdom Age." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-16.html
  - *A caution:* The Pulpit Commentary warns against assuming the Church has completely fulfilled these prophecies, since the New Testament also gives weight to Israel continuing as a nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 17**
- **Jerusalem as God's throne.** The Pulpit Commentary says Jerusalem takes over the ark's title as God's throne. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/3-16.htm
- **"The name of the LORD."** The Pulpit Commentary goes further and treats the "Name" as a Person within God, not just a figure of speech. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 18**
- **"The land of the north."** This means Assyria and Babylonia. The Pulpit Commentary also notes that Israel is converted first, then Judah, and says this detail should not be pressed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 19**
- **"I indeed had said."** The Pulpit Commentary suggests this translation. It reads the verse as God's ideal for Israel: answering his gifts by calling him Father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm
- **Guzik** reads it as a rhetorical question: how could such people receive the land again? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/

**v. 20**
- **"But as a woman…"** The Pulpit Commentary says the word "surely" here takes on a contrasting sense, close to "but surely." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/3.htm

**v. 21**
- **Repentance where the sin happened.** Guzik notes that the weeping comes from the same heights where the idolatry took place. He adds that backsliding is something only God's children can do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/

**v. 22**
- **Come as you are.** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: God does not say "penitent children," and does not require you to heal yourself first before coming back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-3/
- **God heals.** The Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes): "Man repents of sin, but God cures it." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html

**v. 23**
- **False hope exposed.** The Pulpit Commentary (sermon notes) says the hope placed in idols turned out false and in fact caused the ruin it was meant to prevent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-3.html

**v. 24**
- **"That shameful god."** The Hebrew word *bosheth* ("shame") stands in for Baal, as in the names Jerubbaal and Jerubbesheth. Ellicott sees a wasteful sacrifice of animals, and possibly of human life, in the worship of Baal and Molech. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/3-24.htm
- **Another option.** Utley says the mention of "sons and daughters" may point to Molech worship. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-3
- **Gill** adds a less common reading: it may refer to the future shame of rejecting the Messiah, which Israel will confess when it turns to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/3-24.html

**v. 25**
- **A confession with no excuses.** Guzik calls this the broken repentance that should mark God's backsliding children. No excuse or explanation is given. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-3.cfm
